newsitem.title: UK: Barclays shares jump on profits, buy-back.
newsitem.headline: Barclays shares jump on profits, buy-back.

text.p: Shares in British banking giant Barclays rose sharply on Thursday as the bank raised its first half profits and increased its potential for share repurchases this year to 700 million pounds ($1.1 billion) from 500 million.

Barclays profit figures were complicated by the repercussions of Britain's budget but before one-off charges, pre-tax rose eight percent to 1.376 billion pounds, reflecting an 11 percent rise in operating profit.

The figures were within expectations as was a 17 percent dividend rise to 13.5 pence per share and these factors added to the buy-back news and a better performance from the bank's investment banking unit BZW, led to the shares rising 77 pence to stand at 1404.5p by late morning after earlier hitting a record high of 1415p.

Chief executive Martin Taylor said the decision to raise the potential for buy-backs had been taken for the simple reason that the bank's capital position is stronger than he had expected at the beginning of the year.
Barclays has already bought back shares worth 290 million pounds this year and so has potential for a further 410 million pounds of repurchases.

Taylor repeated his aversion to acquisitions for their own sake and said the repurchases were being done as there was no compelling other use for surplus capital although Barclays said it would continue its "highly progressive" dividend policy.
BZW reported lower profits than in last year's first half, 124 million pounds after 148 million, but was up from the disastrous level of 42 million pounds seen in the second half of 1996.
Costs remained high but steady and revenue was better though it admitted a 20 million pounds blemish, lost on equity derivatives trading ahead of the British general election in May.
"What encourages me is that we have lifted our performance and we have a useful pipeline of business going forward," said BZW chief executive Bill Harrison.
Taylor said Barclays has seen its margins tighten in nearly every product area still managed a 30 percent rise in UK banking profits.
"In personal banking, there is pressure," Taylor said in an interview. "Our margins are squeezed in almost every product except mortgages where they are widening slightly as the market recovers."
Barclays' net interest margin was actually wider, climbing to 3.47 percent from 3.24 percent this time last year and 3.42 at the end of 1996.
"The margin is slightly up because we've continued to move the mix of our business towards the higher margin products."
Taylor said new business in mortgages was up 29 percent reflecting the bank's increased preparedness to lend given the better margins in the home finance market.

Barclays said sales of personal loans were particularly buoyant and larger volume had offset tighter margin and Taylor said credit cards had made "reasonable" progress while new business volumes in the mortgage market had risen by 29 percent.
Provisions for bad debts were sharply lower compared to this time last year dipping to 90 million stg from 148 million last year but higher than the 67 million stg seen at the year-end.
Taylor said the main driver for the fall over last year was lower new provisions in business banking.

"We haven't been growing our business book as fast as some of our competitors but we think their growth has been more than obliterated by the provisions they've had," Taylor said. "Our provisions are really very low."
Taylor said provisions were higher in personal banking -- 14 percent up at 168 million pounds -- and that this was due to higher volumes in credit cards and consumer lending.

"But we haven't changed our credit standards, we watch this book very carefully," Taylor said. "Our book is growing about as fast as we are comfortable with. If it were growing much faster, I wouldn't be happy and I do wonder about some of the business some people are putting on."

Taylor said there was more demand as consumers become more confident, "But just because they are more confident, it doesn't necessarily mean that they are more able to service the debt. That's what we have to work on."
Costs overall in the bank were higher than in the first half of 1996 but lower than in the second six months and Taylor said that in the long-term he can see scope for cutting costs further.
"At the moment were are trying to offer our customers more choice and more convenience which means adding to costs in some areas," Taylor said.
